---
title: "Puzzle #121 — Two Eggs, 100 Floors, Exactly 14 Drops"
description: "A fully explained mathematical puzzle with symbols, small numbers, derivation and proof."
---

## 1. Turn the story into a precise problem

A special fragile item can be dropped from floors of a 100-story building. It breaks above an unknown threshold. You have two identical items; broken ones cannot be reused. How few drops GUARANTEE identifying the highest safe floor?

## 2. Check a small case first

If you used the first item at floor 50 and it broke, only one item would remain and you might need 49 sequential checks. Equal jump sizes are not optimal: the jumps should get SHORTER as the remaining drop allowance shrinks.

## 3. Express the key relationship

$$
H(d,2)=\frac{d(d+1)}{2}
$$

**What every symbol means:** H(d,2) is the largest number of consecutive floors whose threshold can always be determined with d drops and two items. d(d+1)/2 is the sum d+(d−1)+...+1.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Try d=13: 13×14/2=**91**, too few for 100 floors. Try d=14: 14×15/2=**105**, enough. Therefore the optimum worst-case allowance is **14 drops**.

## 4. Derive the result — why it must be true

Use decreasing jump sizes. First try floor 14. If it breaks, examine floors 1 through 13 sequentially with the remaining item: at most 14 total drops. If it survives, next try floor 14+13=27; after a break there are at most 12 intermediate floors to check. Then jump +12 to 39, +11 to 50, +10 to 60, and so on. Every case fits within 14 drops.

## 5. Validate the answer

The recurrence behind this bound is H(d,e)=1+H(d−1,e−1)+H(d−1,e): one test floor plus the floors below if it breaks plus the floors above if it survives. With one item, H(d,1)=d because you must test from bottom up. Substituting e=2 and expanding yields 1+2+...+d. Since 13 drops cover at most 91 floors, no 13-drop strategy can guarantee success for all 100.

## 6. Generalise and identify the limitation

For 36 floors and two items, what is the smallest d with d(d+1)/2≥36? Try d=8 (36) and d=7 (28). Explain why eight is necessary and sufficient.

## 7. Try another example

Recurrence, worst-case optimality, triangular numbers, adaptive experiment design.
